reasons: [traceability/major] D1 [edgeCasesAndFailureModes[3]; compare criteriaAssessments C1.strengths[0], C6.assessment, CL10] The edge case says shared control-plane or global services (DNS, identity, certificate issuance) can 'fail and take down both regions, as the Oct 2025 DNS-automation event shows can happen'. E10 does not support this. It describes the Oct 2025 event as 'region-scoped': an empty DNS record for DynamoDB's regional endpoint in us-east-1. It says nothing about two regions going down together. The draft also uses the same event in C1, C3, C6 and CL10 as its main example of a single-region loss that multi-region would protect against. So one event is cited for two opposite points, and the cross-region claim has no support. This matters because a reader could take it as evidence that active-active would fail in exactly the tail scenario that is its main justification.

[coverage/major] D2 [criteriaAssessments C3.mechanisms, C6.mechanisms; CL8; furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion] The main unknown, Halvorsen's fees and contract value, is left open. There is no threshold or sensitivity analysis to bound the decision. The only break-even (CL8) covers credits alone with a first-tier credit every month. That is a strawman: the real case for the project is losing the customer or a rare long regional outage, not routine credits. The draft could have computed: (a) the regional-outage frequency at which expected credits plus churn loss reach about $492k/yr plus one engineer-year, using CL10's 19-step credit per event; and (b) the annual contract value at which avoiding one customer-loss event every N years pays for the project. Without this the decision-maker cannot tell how big a fee or termination clause would flip the verdict, even though the draft lists those as research that could change the conclusion. C3 (20%) and C6 (8%) are therefore assessed only qualitatively.

[alternatives_counterarguments/major] D3 [alternatives[3]; C6.mechanisms; counterarguments[0].response; tradeoffs[0]] The recommended hedge, warm standby or pilot light, is presented with upsides only. The draft does not check whether warm standby's RTO ('in minutes'; pilot light 'tens of minutes', per E14), plus detection and decision time, would keep a regional failover inside the 21.6-minute monthly budget or under the 64.8-minute first credit tier. Pilot light at tens of minutes could plausibly breach both. The draft also calls 'keeps the ledger single-writer' a pure benefit, but it does not mention that async-replicated standby means RPO above zero, i.e. possible loss of committed financial ledger transactions on failover. For a ledger that is the strongest argument for active-active or synchronous replication, and the draft leaves it out. Failover-drill cost and the risk that a rarely used standby does not work when needed are also absent. The comparison with active-active is therefore one-sided.
D1 and D3 have remedy 'both' (Oct 2025 event scope; warm-standby RTO/RPO realism); D2/D4-D7 reanalysis

[evidence_sufficiency/major] D1 [verdict (final sentences on lower bounds); C3.mechanisms ('which E21/E22 cast doubt on'); CL17] The verdict is new in draft-2. It says the break-even thresholds assume active-active would avoid the whole regional event, 'which is doubtful: recent large outages have spread through shared global layers that a second region at the same provider would still depend on.' The evidence does not support 'doubtful'. CL20 says 'the extent of data-plane impact in other regions is not established', and E21's own limitations say the snippets cover IAM 'updates' (control-plane changes), not authentication or data planes in other regions. The two other examples are not regional events. Google Cloud June 2025 (E23) and Azure Front Door Oct 2025 (E24) were global-layer failures, so they say nothing about whether a second region would have survived a region-scoped trigger like us-east-1 Oct 2025. That scenario is exactly what active-active is built for. E33 also describes itself as 'anecdotes, not a base rate'. Using global-outage anecdotes to discount active-active's main benefit against regional outages mixes two failure classes, and states the conclusion with more confidence than the snippet-level evidence allows. A decision-maker could undervalue regional redundancy as a result. The verdict does not need this point: it holds on C1, C2 and C5 alone.

[reasoning_validity/major] D2 [CL17; K18; C3.mechanisms (b); practicalImplications[5]; furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion[0]; verdict] The new sensitivity analysis calls all its thresholds 'lower bounds'. That holds for the credit thresholds (K16, K17): they assume uncapped credits, full unavailability and no engineering cost, and each relaxation raises the threshold. It does not hold for the churn threshold (K18, about $2.46M/yr). K18 assumes losing Halvorsen forfeits exactly one year of contract value. If the customer would otherwise stay several years, the forfeited value is larger and the threshold falls (about $820k/yr for a 3-year remaining lifetime). Using revenue rather than margin pushes the other way. The 'one loss every 5 years' frequency is arbitrary and not tied to any evidence (E12 gives no base rate). So $2.46M/yr is an illustrative point estimate under arbitrary assumptions, not a bound. Yet practicalImplications and furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion tell the decision-maker to compare the real contract value against it. A contract worth, say, $1.5M/yr with a multi-year relationship could wrongly look as if it fails to clear the bar.
D1/D2 major (overstated 'doubtful'; churn threshold mislabelled lower bound), remedy reanalysis
